semantics.note: A firm conditional 'would' that keeps the 'assuming they actually became useful' antecedent. The 'they' refers to Google, Amazon or Microsoft. The startup-affordability premise is left out, but the scored consequence is captured faithfully.

contract.note: Reading the claim as eventual consolidation with no deadline is charitable and ordinary. The bar for 'useful' (benefit shown in one real application) is low, but it does not change the result. An immediate-dependence reading would make the local-LLM evidence decisive. The contract flags this.

evidence.note: A dated NBER field study showing practical benefit from an LLM assistant. It bears on the antecedent (usefulness), not on the predicted control outcome.
GPT4All's July 2024 release runs Meta's Llama locally with no API calls. This challenges the necessity premise, but it is not a decisive event against eventual universal control.

reviews.rationale: This is a firm conditional forecast with no deadline. The usefulness antecedent is plausibly met. The packet has no comprehensive control audit and no decisive event that either establishes or rules out universal control by the three firms. Local-LLM tools are counterexamples today, but under the contract they do not settle an undated forecast.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own newsletter post.

semantics.note: 'It would turn' is a firm consequence of 'the alternative' to a minimal-value fad. The antecedent is kept. His hedge ('will likely prove to be a transient fad') applies to the fad belief, not to the conditional consequence.

contract.note: Treating 'parasitic' as unscored and reading 'a cut' as a required model or compute payment are both fair. Measuring 'the alternative' by practical usefulness may set a lower bar than his 'minimal value' contrast implies, but with no deadline the result does not change.

evidence.note: A 2023-24 workplace Copilot experiment, available in August 2026 before the cutoff, showing time savings. It bears on the antecedent, not on the payment-dependence outcome.
LM Studio's August 2024 release runs local models offline. This weakens universal payment dependence today, but it is not a complete payment audit and not a decisive event.

reviews.rationale: This is a firm conditional forecast about future market structure, with no deadline. The packet does not show universal required payments to a handful of firms, and no decisive event rules that state out. Local-model tools are present counterexamples but do not resolve an undated forecast under the contract.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own newsletter post.

semantics.note: A present-tense claim that the four firms collectively monopolize data centers and access to specialized GPUs. The normalisation is faithful.

contract.note: Reading 'monopolize' by four firms as effective collective control that obstructs competition is an ordinary, fair reading. It is neither literal exclusivity nor mere concentration. Q2 2024 is a reasonable period for an undated present-state claim.

evidence.note: Synergy's Q2 2024 shares of general cloud-services revenue (Amazon, Microsoft, Google). This is a proxy only: it is not AI capacity or GPU access and omits Meta.
A CoreWeave company disclosure (May 2024) of 14 data centers as an independent GPU cloud. It gives no market share, so it does not show competitive-scale independence.
Oracle disclosure (June 2024) of AI customers on OCI. The OpenAI deal extends Microsoft Azure, which limits any inference of independence. No share data.

reviews.rationale: The packet shows heavy concentration in general cloud revenue and the existence of some independent GPU suppliers. It has no AI-specific measure of capacity or GPU access to establish either effective collective control or material independent capacity at competitive scale.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own newsletter post.

semantics.note: Causal claim: compute and cash requirements are why most companies cannot compete at scale. 'In the LLM market' follows from 'these models' in context.

contract.note: Limiting the claim to firms developing general-purpose LLMs and requiring that resource barriers caused exclusion is a fair, ordinary reading. 'Most companies' leaves the population undefined, as the contract flags.

evidence.note: The CMA (April 2024) says substantial compute is critical for capable models and that big tech has greater access. This supports the mechanism, but not the 'most companies excluded' part.
The same CMA paper calls open-source models an important competitive force. This qualifies general exclusion but does not show that most firms could compete at scale.

reviews.rationale: The evidence supports the claimed resource barrier, but the packet has no denominator of potential competitors. It also does not separate compute and cash from other barriers, so it cannot establish that the requirements excluded most competitors. Open-model competition qualifies the claim but does not refute it.
